steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) are both nucleic acids built from nucleotide sub-units, but they differ in four main respects: chemical composition, structure, stability, and biological role.

1. Chemical composition  
   • Sugar: DNA contains deoxyribose, which lacks an oxygen atom at the 2′ carbon; RNA contains ribose, which has that 2′-OH group.  
   • Bases: Both use adenine (A), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). DNA uses thymine (T), but RNA uses uracil (U) in its place.  
   • Phosphate backbone: Both have a phosphate group linking the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ carbon of the next, but the extra 2′-OH in RNA makes its backbone more reactive.

2. Structure  
   • DNA is normally double-stranded, forming a long, stable antiparallel double helix (B-form in cells).  
   • RNA is typically single-stranded and folds back on itself to make complex 3-D shapes (hairpins, loops, pseudoknots). Some viral RNAs can be double-stranded, but cellular RNA is mostly single.  

3. Stability and localization  
   • DNA’s lack of the 2′-OH and its helix-shielded bases make it chemically and enzymatically more stable; it is the long-term genetic repository and is mostly confined to the nucleus (plus mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is less stable—its 2′-OH can participate in self-cleavage, and abundant RNases readily degrade it. That transient nature suits its roles as messenger and catalyst. RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (or nucleoid) but functions throughout the cell (cytoplasm, ribosome, spliceosome, etc.).

4. Biological roles  
   • DNA stores hereditary information and is faithfully replicated during cell division.  
   • RNA conveys and uses that information: mRNA carries coding sequences to ribosomes; rRNA and tRNA form the machinery of translation; regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA) fine-tune gene expression; some RNAs (ribozymes, snRNAs) act as enzymes.

In short: DNA is the durable, double-stranded blueprint written in A-T/G-C pairs with deoxyribose; RNA is the versatile, usually single-stranded working copy/catalyst written in A-U/G-C with ribose.
